readerTitle: The countdown timer that resets every night
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션: 40개 매장을 둔 가정용품 체인의 사내 마케팅팀 (매장 + 온라인몰) · 모든 상황과 수치는 설명용
insight: 설득과 조작을 가르는 기준은 이것이다. 고객이 우리가 하는 일을 전부 알아도 그 방법이 여전히 통하는가. 진짜 마감과 진짜 인기는 그래도 통하고, 가짜는 들키는 순간 신뢰까지 함께 잃는다.
misconception: 효과만 있으면 어떤 설득 기법이든 괜찮다. 또는 반대로, 설득 기법을 쓰는 것 자체가 조작이다.

sources.text: 모든 인물, 회사, 상황, 수치는 설명용 가상 사례
설득 원칙(사회적 증거, 희소성·긴급성, 프레이밍)은 이 유닛의 앞선 레슨에서 다룬 일반 개념

factChecks.note: 가상 시뮬레이션이라 실제 통계나 연구 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다. '40개 매장', '30곳', '$19', '3년 보증' 등은 모두 설명용 숫자입니다.
허위 재고 표시나 가짜 카운트다운의 법적 문제는 국가마다 달라 다루지 않았습니다. 본문에는 신뢰와 고객 반응, 다른 팀으로 넘어가는 비용만 적었습니다.
테이크어웨이의 개념 연결을 확인하세요. 마감 → 긴급성(MKT-03-02), 매장 표지판 → 사회적 증거(MKT-03-01), 재고 표시 → 희소성(MKT-03-02), 보증 문구 → 프레이밍(MKT-03-06).

cards.title: The countdown timer that resets every night
body: You lead the marketing team at a home-goods chain with 40 stores and an online shop. It's the winter heater sale, and your director wants sales up sharply this month.
This week you face four calls. Each one tempts you with a trick that would probably work. Once.

image.label: A marketing manager's desk with four sticky notes and a countdown timer
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 사무실 책상 위 노트북 화면에 'Ends in 02:00:00' 카운트다운, 옆 모니터 테두리에 포스트잇 4장(Deadline, Signs, Stock, Warranty). 창밖은 겨울. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The sale really ends January 31.
body: Your agency suggests a website timer: "Sale ends in 2 hours!" It restarts for every new visitor. What do you run?

options.feedback: Clicks jump today. But customers who come back see the timer start over, and they stop believing any deadline you set, including real ones.

options.text: A clear real deadline: "Sale ends Sunday, Jan 31"
options.feedback: A true deadline gives people a real reason to decide now. It still works if they know exactly what you're doing.
Honest, but you throw away a true fact that would help customers stop putting it off.

cards.title: Say you chose the real deadline. Now, the shelves.
body: Store managers want "Bestseller" signs. One heater truly sells most in 30 of your 40 stores. Another model is badly overstocked.

image.label: Two heaters on a store shelf with different signs
image.brief: 매장 선반 위 히터 두 대. 왼쪽은 'Our most-bought heater this winter' 표지판, 오른쪽은 'Now $20 off' 가격표. 따뜻한 조명, 상표 없는 가상 제품.

options.text: Put "Bestseller" on the overstocked model to clear it
options.feedback: It may move boxes. But staff know the truth, and a customer who asks a clerk can find out the sign is false.

options.text: "Our most-bought heater this winter" on the true top seller, a plain price cut on the overstock
options.feedback: Real popularity helps unsure shoppers. The overstock moves on an honest reason: a lower price.
Not quite a lie, but it says nothing. When every sign says the same thing, shoppers learn to ignore all of them.

cards.title: Say you chose real signs. Now, a request from above.
body: The regional director wants "Only 2 left!" on every clearance item online. The warehouse has hundreds of each.

options.text: Add it to every item. It's the director's call
options.feedback: Orders may rise this week. Then customers notice the same "2 left" for days, and reviews start calling you out.

options.text: Offer a live stock count that appears only when stock is truly low
options.feedback: The director gets a scarcity tool, and it's true every time it shows. You win the argument by offering something better.

options.text: Refuse and leave the pages as they are
options.feedback: Honest, but you give the director nothing. The request often comes back, and next time without you.

cards.title: Say you offered the live count. Last call: the warranty.
body: Finance wants the $19 extended warranty box ticked by default online, under the line "Don't risk a broken heater."

options.text: Pre-tick it with the fear line
options.feedback: Warranty sales rise. So do refund requests and angry calls, and that cost lands on the service team, not yours.

options.text: Leave it unticked: "3 years of repairs for $19. Your heater already has 1 year."
options.feedback: Fewer sales than the pre-ticked box, but each buyer chose it with the full facts. Almost none come back asking for refunds.
No pressure at all, but customers who wanted extra cover lose an easy option.

cards.title: Persuasion vs manipulation
body: Every best choice passed one test: **would it still work if the customer saw exactly what you were doing?**

A real deadline, a real bestseller and a plain warranty offer all pass. They help people act on something true. A resetting timer or fake stock only works while nobody notices. That's **manipulation**: it borrows trust and pays it back with interest.

image.label: Glass box test: honest tactics still work when seen
image.brief: 투명한 유리 상자 두 개. 왼쪽 상자 안에는 'Ends Jan 31' 달력이 그대로 빛나고, 오른쪽 상자 안 리셋 타이머는 금이 가며 꺼짐. 단순한 인포그래픽 톤.

cards.softwareNote: The same test applies to fake "5 people viewing this plan" pop-ups, trials that quietly turn into paid plans, and hard-to-find cancel buttons. If users would object once they saw how it works, it's a trick.

cards.title: Honest can lose the first week.
body: The tricks often win on this month's sales number. Their costs show up later and elsewhere: returns, refunds, complaints, customers who stop coming back.
Inside a company, that makes manipulation look smart to one team while another pays. Report those costs next to sales so the whole picture is in the room.

cards.title: Use what's true, and let customers see it.
body: Each call this week used an idea from this unit, in its honest form:
cards.callout: **Try it today:** pick one message you use to sell. Ask: would it still work if the customer knew exactly why it's there?
cards.next: Next · You've finished Persuasion. A new unit starts tomorrow.
